By the end you will be able to Download a real dataset and explore it in R Build plots with the ggplot2 grammar: data → aesthetics → geoms → layers Customise plots with colour, shape, size, facets and themes Make plots interactive with plotly Use an AI assistant to write, explain and debug R code — and check what it gives you New to R or ggplot2? Using AI in this workshop AI assistants are great for learning R: they explain error messages, suggest the next line, and help you iterate on a plot much faster. We treat them as a normal part of the toolkit — not cheating. Good things to ask an AI “Explain this R error and how to fix it: <paste error>” “Write ggplot2 code to plot x vs y coloured by group from a data frame called data.” “How do I make this ggplot interactive with plotly?” “What does aes() do here, in simple terms?” Three rules when using AI Run it and read it — never paste code you don’t understand. Ask the AI to explain anything unclear. Check the output — AI can invent column names or functions. If a plot looks wrong, it probably is. Learn from it — the goal is that you can do it next time, with or without the AI. Look out for 🤖 Ask your AI tips in the exercises — small prompts you can try.

2 Get the data Our very first step, together: get the data and look at it. Everything we plot today comes from this one experiment, so let’s meet it first. 📌 The big idea of this workshop: a plot is an answer to a question. Before every plot we’ll ask a biological question — and then build the figure that answers it.

The experiment We’ll work with real RNA-seq data from Staphylococcus aureus (strain USA-500), grown in two lifestyles: Biofilm — cells living in a sticky, surface-attached community Planktonic — cells swimming freely in liquid The biological question behind the whole dataset: Which genes does S. aureus turn up or down when it switches from free-living (planktonic) to a biofilm? We have three files in the data/ folder: File What it is gene_counts.tsv how strongly each gene is expressed in each sample metadata.tsv which lifestyle / timepoint each sample belongs to DE_biofilm_vs_planktonic_24h.tsv the result of a statistical test: how much each gene changed (biofilm vs planktonic, 24 h)

Load it We’ll use the tidyverse for everything today. Read the three files: library(tidyverse) counts <- read_tsv("data/gene_counts.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE) meta <- read_tsv("data/metadata.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE) de <- read_tsv("data/DE_biofilm_vs_planktonic_24h.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE) 📌 Remember: read_tsv() reads tab-separated files. Its cousin read_csv() reads comma-separated ones.

First look Never plot data you haven’t looked at. Get a feel for each table first. The questions we’ll answer today Each of the next sections takes one biological question and builds the plot that answers it: Can I trust and compare my samples? → distributions per sample Do biofilm and planktonic samples separate? → PCA How does a single gene behave? → boxplot with the data points Which genes changed the most? → the volcano plot Can others explore the result themselves? → an interactive version Let’s start asking. 👉

3 The grammar of graphics Before we touch the real data, let’s learn the one idea that powers every plot in ggplot2: the grammar of graphics. Every plot is built from three pieces: data → aesthetics (aes: which column goes on x, y, colour…) → geom (how to draw it) We’ll learn it on a tiny built-in dataset, mpg (fuel economy of cars), then use it on our bacteria. library(tidyverse) head(mpg) ## 4 Can I compare my samples? The question: before comparing conditions, are the samples themselves comparable — or is one wildly different? The plot that answers it: the distribution of counts per sample. First, reshape the counts to tidy form (one row per gene × sample) and attach the sample info: counts_long <- counts %>% pivot_longer(-c(gene_id, gene_name), names_to = "sample", values_to = "count") %>% left_join(meta, by = "sample") counts_long ## # A tibble: 93,696 × 9 ## gene_id gene_name sample count strain reference lifestyle timepoint replicate ## <chr> <chr> <chr> <dbl> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <dbl> ## 1 SAUSA3… SAUSA300… USA50… 1453 USA500 NRS385 Biofilm 10h 1 ## 2 SAUSA3… SAUSA300… USA50… 1440 USA500 NRS385 Biofilm 10h 2 ## 3 SAUSA3… SAUSA300… USA50… 1483 USA500 NRS385 Biofilm 10h 3 ## 4 SAUSA3… SAUSA300… USA50… 1446 USA500 NRS385 Biofilm 10h 4 ## 5 SAUSA3… SAUSA300… USA50… 520. USA500 NRS385 Biofilm 24h 1 ## 6 SAUSA3… SAUSA300… USA50… 511 USA500 NRS385 Biofilm 24h 2 ## 7 SAUSA3… SAUSA300… USA50… 485. USA500 NRS385 Biofilm 24h 3 ## 8 SAUSA3… SAUSA300… USA50… 503 USA500 NRS385 Biofilm 24h 4 ## 9 SAUSA3… SAUSA300… USA50… 500. USA500 NRS385 Biofilm 24h 5 ## 10 SAUSA3… SAUSA300… USA50… 520 USA500 NRS385 Biofilm 24h 6 ## # ℹ 93,686 more rows A boxplot per sample, coloured by lifestyle (counts are very skewed, so we plot them on a log scale): ggplot(counts_long, aes(x = sample, y = log10(count + 1), fill = lifestyle)) + geom_boxplot() + coord_flip() + labs(x = NULL, y = "log10(count + 1)") If the boxes line up at similar heights, the samples are comparable. 👍 📌 Principle: skewed data (like counts) needs a log scale, or one huge value flattens everything else. 👉 Your turn Show the same information as a density plot instead of boxplots: one curve per sample, coloured by lifestyle. (Hint: geom_density() with aes(group = sample).) Solution ggplot(counts_long, aes(x = log10(count + 1), group = sample, colour = lifestyle)) + geom_density() 🤖 Ask your AI: “Why do we add 1 before taking log10 of RNA-seq counts?”

5 Do biofilm and planktonic separate? The question: do the samples group by lifestyle, the way we’d hope? The plot that answers it: a PCA, which squeezes thousands of genes into two axes so we can see which samples are alike. Build a gene × sample matrix, log-transform it, and run the PCA on the samples: mat <- counts %>% select(-gene_name) %>% column_to_rownames("gene_id") %>% as.matrix() logmat <- log2(mat + 1) logmat <- logmat[rowSums(mat) > 0, ] # drop genes that are always zero pca <- prcomp(t(logmat)) # samples in rows for PCA # how much variance each axis explains var_pct <- round(100 * pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2), 1) pca_df <- as.data.frame(pca$x) %>% rownames_to_column("sample") %>% left_join(meta, by = "sample") Now the plot — colour by lifestyle, shape by timepoint: ggplot(pca_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = lifestyle, shape = timepoint)) + geom_point(size = 3) + labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", var_pct[1], "%)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", var_pct[2], "%)")) If biofilm and planktonic land in separate clusters, lifestyle is a strong signal in the data — exactly what we want before looking for changed genes. 📌 Principle: colour and shape let one plot answer two questions at once (here: lifestyle and timepoint). 👉 Your turn Does maturation (timepoint) matter too? Re-colour the points by timepoint instead of lifestyle and see whether the timepoints separate. Solution ggplot(pca_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = timepoint, shape = lifestyle)) + geom_point(size = 3) + labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", var_pct[1], "%)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", var_pct[2], "%)")) 🤖 Ask your AI: “In a PCA of RNA-seq samples, what does it mean if PC1 explains 80% of the variance?”
6 How does a single gene behave?

6 How does a single gene behave? The question: take one interesting gene — how different is it between biofilm and planktonic? The plot that answers it: a boxplot with the data points shown. Let’s pick the gene that changed the most (we’ll meet the full result in the next chapter): top_gene <- de %>% filter(padj < 0.05) %>% slice_max(abs(log2FoldChange), n = 1) %>% pull(gene_id) top_gene ## [1] "SAUSA300_RS11095" Plot its expression at 24 h, one box per lifestyle, with every replicate shown on top: counts_long %>% filter(gene_id == top_gene, timepoint == "24h") %>% ggplot(aes(x = lifestyle, y = log10(count + 1), colour = lifestyle)) + geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) + geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 2) + labs(title = top_gene, x = NULL, y = "log10(count + 1)") 📌 Principle: always show the actual data points on top of a boxplot — with only a few replicates, the box alone can hide the real story. 👉 Your turn Pick a different gene (any gene_id from the de table) and plot it the same way. Does it go up or down in biofilm? Solution my_gene <- "SAUSA300_RS00670" # change me counts_long %>% filter(gene_id == my_gene, timepoint == "24h") %>% ggplot(aes(x = lifestyle, y = log10(count + 1), colour = lifestyle)) + geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) + geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 2) + labs(title = my_gene) 🤖 Ask your AI: “Why show individual points with geom_jitter instead of just a boxplot when there are only a few replicates?”

7 What changed? The volcano plot The big question of the whole experiment: which genes change between biofilm and planktonic? The plot that answers it — and the one you’ll walk out able to make — is the volcano plot: fold change on x, significance on y. Prepare the data. (A few genes have an adjusted p-value of exactly 0; we replace those with the smallest non-zero value so they can be plotted.) de_plot <- de %>% mutate( padj = ifelse(padj == 0, min(padj[padj > 0], na.rm = TRUE), padj), status = case_when( padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange > 1 ~ "Up in biofilm", padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange < -1 ~ "Down in biofilm", TRUE ~ "Not significant" ) ) The volcano: volcano <- ggplot(de_plot, aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj), colour = status)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.6) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("Up in biofilm" = "firebrick", "Down in biofilm" = "steelblue", "Not significant" = "grey70")) + labs(x = "log2 fold change (biofilm vs planktonic)", y = "-log10(adjusted p-value)", colour = NULL) volcano ## Warning: Removed 45 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range ## (`geom_point()`). Far-right red points = strongly up in biofilm; far-left blue = strongly down. High up the y-axis = most confident. That single picture answers the experiment. 📌 Principle: a good plot encodes two things at once here — effect size (x) and confidence (y) — so the eye finds the important genes instantly.

Make it explorable One line turns it interactive — hover any point to see which gene it is: library(plotly) ggplotly(volcano) 👉 Your turn Add dashed threshold lines to the static volcano so the cutoffs are visible: vertical lines at log2FoldChange = −1 and 1, and a horizontal line at the p = 0.05 level. (Hint: geom_vline(), geom_hline(), linetype = "dashed".) Solution volcano + geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed") + geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed") 🤖 Ask your AI: “On a volcano plot, what do points in the top-left and top-right corners represent biologically?”

8 Challenge: your publication-ready volcano This is the hands-on hour. You’ve built every piece — now make a volcano plot you’d be proud to put in a paper. Use your AI assistant freely. Your mission: start from de_plot and produce a polished volcano that: shows dashed threshold lines (fold change ±1, p = 0.05); labels the ~10 most significant genes (hint: the ggrepel package); has a clean theme, a clear title, and readable, colourblind-friendly colours; is one you can explain to a colleague in a sentence. Everything you need is already loaded: de_plot, volcano, and the tidyverse. 📌 Remember the big idea: the plot is the answer to “which genes change between biofilm and planktonic?” — make that answer jump out. 🤖 Ask your AI (ideas): “How do I label only the top 10 genes on a ggplot volcano with ggrepel?” · “Suggest a colourblind-friendly palette for up/down/ns.” · “How do I make this figure look publication-ready?” — then run it, read it, and check it does what you expect. One possible solution library(ggrepel) top_genes <- de_plot %>% filter(status != "Not significant") %>% slice_max(-log10(padj), n = 10) ggplot(de_plot, aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj))) + geom_point(aes(colour = status), alpha = 0.6) + geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") + geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") + geom_text_repel(data = top_genes, aes(label = gene_id), size = 3, max.overlaps = Inf) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("Up in biofilm" = "#D55E00", "Down in biofilm" = "#0072B2", "Not significant" = "grey70")) + labs(title = "S. aureus: biofilm vs planktonic (24 h)", x = "log2 fold change", y = "-log10(adjusted p-value)", colour = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

Showcase Share your figure with the room — what’s your favourite gene, and what does it tell you about how S. aureus lives in a biofilm? 🎉 Going further If you finish early: label genes by name instead of ID, make the plot interactive with ggplotly(), or try a heatmap of your top genes across all samples.
